fanoutqa_009791.x:
Harvard University :: Organization and administration :: Governance :: chunk_0013
See also: [Harvard Board of Overseers](/wiki/Harvard_Board_of_Overseers "Harvard Board of Overseers"), [President and Fellows of Harvard College](/wiki/President_and_Fellows_of_Harvard_College "President and Fellows of Harvard College"), and [President of Harvard University](/wiki/President_of_Harvard_University "President of Harvard University")

Harvard is governed by a combination of its [Board of Overseers](/wiki/Harvard_Board_of_Overseers "Harvard Board of Overseers") and the [President and Fellows of Harvard College](/wiki/President_and_Fellows_of_Harvard_College "President and Fellows of Harvard College"), which is also known as the Harvard Corporation. These two bodies, in turn, appoint the [president of Harvard University](/wiki/President_of_Harvard_University "President of Harvard University").[[93]](#cite_note-94)

There are 16,000 staff and faculty,[[94]](#cite_note-95) including 2,400 professors, lecturers, and instructors in the colleges proper,[[95]](#cite_note-96) plus another >10,400 academic appointments in affiliated teaching hospitals)[[96]](#cite_note-97)

As of 2025, Harvard differs radically from its peer universities in two important ways. First, Harvard does not make its governing statutes publicly available, meaning that members of the Harvard community interested in reform must first persuade the university to give them a copy of those documents. Second, Harvard does not have an [academic senate](/wiki/Academic_senate "Academic senate") like most of its peers, although it is currently attempting to create one.[[97]](#cite_note-Heller-98)

Main article: [Claims to the first powered flight](/wiki/Claims_to_the_first_powered_flight "Claims to the first powered flight")

Further information: [Early flying machines](/wiki/Early_flying_machines "Early flying machines") and [Aviation in the pioneer era](/wiki/Aviation_in_the_pioneer_era "Aviation in the pioneer era")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/08/US_pilots_certificate_back.jpg/250px-US_pilots_certificate_back.jpg)](/wiki/File:US_pilots_certificate_back.jpg)

Back of the [US Airman Certificate](/wiki/Pilot_certification_in_the_United_States "Pilot certification in the United States") with a picture of the Wright brothers

First powered flight claims are made for [Clément Ader](/wiki/Cl%C3%A9ment_Ader "Clément Ader"), [Gustave Whitehead](/wiki/Gustave_Whitehead "Gustave Whitehead"), [Richard Pearse](/wiki/Richard_Pearse "Richard Pearse"), and [Karl Jatho](/wiki/Karl_Jatho "Karl Jatho") for their variously documented tests in years prior to and including 1903. Claims that the first true flight occurred after 1903 are made for [Traian Vuia](/wiki/Traian_Vuia "Traian Vuia") and [Alberto Santos-Dumont](/wiki/Alberto_Santos-Dumont "Alberto Santos-Dumont"). Supporters of the post-Wright pioneers argue that techniques used by the Wright brothers disqualify them as first to make successful airplane flights. Those techniques were: A launch rail; skids instead of wheels; a headwind at takeoff; and a catapult after 1903. Supporters of the Wright brothers argue that proven, repeated, controlled, and sustained flights by the brothers entitle them to credit as inventors of the airplane, regardless of those techniques.[[191]](#cite_note-202)

The aviation historian [C. H. Gibbs-Smith](/wiki/Charles_Harvard_Gibbs-Smith "Charles Harvard Gibbs-Smith") was a supporter of the Wrights' claim to primacy in flight. He wrote that a barn door can be made to "fly" for a short distance if enough energy is applied to it; he determined that the very limited flight experiments of Ader, Vuia, and others were "powered hops" instead of fully controlled flights.[[192]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEGibbs-Smith1985xii,_60,_

The series is known for its original songs that appear in almost every episode since the first season episode "[Flop Starz](/wiki/Flop_Starz "Flop Starz")". Disney's executives particularly enjoyed the episode's song "Gitchee, Gitchee Goo" and requested that a song appear in each subsequent episode.[[5]](#cite_note-AM2-8) The music earned the series a total of four [Emmy](/wiki/Emmy_Awards "Emmy Awards") nominations: two [Primetime Creative Arts](/wiki/Creative_Arts_Emmy_Awards "Creative Arts Emmy Awards") nominations in [2008](/wiki/60th_Primetime_Creative_Arts_Emmy_Awards "60th Primetime Creative Arts Emmy Awards") (for the main title theme and for the song "I Ain't Got Rhythm" from the episode "[Dude, We're Getting the Band Back Together](/wiki/Dude,_We%27re_Getting_the_Band_Back_Together "Dude, We're Getting the Band Back Together")")[[35]](#cite_note-EmmySearch-38) and two [Daytime Creative Arts](/wiki/Daytime_Emmy_Awards "Daytime Emmy Awards") nominations in [2010](/wiki/37th_Daytime_Emmy_Awards "37th Daytime Emmy Awards") (for the song "Come Home Perry" from the episode "Oh, There You Are, Perry" and the original score by [Danny Jacob](/wiki/Danny_Jacob "Danny Jacob")).

> "Phineas and Ferb gave us a chance to write a song for every single episode, starting with the second episode, Flop Starz. [...]   
> Every episode since then has a song in it. It's not always the characters singing onscreen – they don't break into song just to advance the plot. The music doesn't come out of nowhere, sometimes it's just a montage over action. We've done every genre known to man: ABBA, Broadway show tunes, 16th-century madrigals"

— [Dan Povenmire](/wiki/Dan_Povenmire "Dan Povenmire") on the songs featured in every episode since "[Flop Starz](/wiki/Flop_Starz "Flop Starz")".[[5]](#cite_note-AM2-8)

At West Point in 1922

Taylor was born in [Keytesville, Missouri](/wiki/Keytesville,_Missouri "Keytesville, Missouri"), the only child of attorney John Earle Maxwell Taylor and Pearle (Davenport) Taylor. He was raised in [Kansas City](/wiki/Kansas_City,_Missouri "Kansas City, Missouri"), graduated from [Northeast High School](/wiki/Northeast_High_School_(Missouri) "Northeast High School (Missouri)"), and attended [Kansas City Polytechnic Institute](/wiki/Metropolitan_Community_College_(Missouri) "Metropolitan Community College (Missouri)"). In 1918, he passed competitive examinations for Congressional appointment by [William Patterson Borland](/wiki/William_Patterson_Borland "William Patterson Borland") to either the [United States Military Academy](/wiki/United_States_Military_Academy "United States Military Academy") or [United States Naval Academy](/wiki/United_States_Naval_Academy "United States Naval Academy") and then passed the Military Academy entrance examination. Taylor attended West Point, graduated fourth in the Class of 1922, and was [commissioned](/wiki/Officer_(armed_forces) "Officer (armed forces)") as a [second lieutenant](/wiki/Second_lieutenant "Second lieutenant") in the [U.S. Army Corps of Engineers](/wiki/United_States_Army_Corps_of_Engineers "United States Army Corps of Engineers"). He served in [Hawaii](/wiki/Hawaii "Hawaii") with the 3rd Engineers from 1923 to 1926.

Taylor transferred to the [Field Artillery](/wiki/Field_Artillery_Branch_(United_States) "Field Artillery Branch (United States)") and, from 1926 to 1927, served with the 10th Field Artillery, receiving promotion to [first lieutenant](/wiki/First_lieutenant "First lieutenant"). * The High Republic: Under the protection of the Jedi, the Republic grows into a [golden age](/wiki/Golden_age "Golden age"). [Saturn](/wiki/Saturn "Saturn") has [292 moons](/wiki/Moons_of_Saturn "Moons of Saturn") with known orbits announced; 66 of them have received permanent designations, and 63 have been named. Most of them are quite small. Seven moons are large enough to be in [hydrostatic equilibrium](/wiki/Hydrostatic_equilibrium "Hydrostatic equilibrium"), including [Titan](/wiki/Titan_(moon) "Titan (moon)"), the second largest moon in the Solar System. Including these large moons, 24 of Saturn's moons are regular, and traditionally named after [Titans](/wiki/Titan_(mythology) "Titan (mythology)") or other figures associated with the mythological [Saturn](/wiki/Saturn_(mythology) "Saturn (mythology)"). The remaining moons are irregular, and classified by their orbital characteristics into [Inuit](/wiki/Saturn%27s_Inuit_group_of_satellites "Saturn's Inuit group of satellites"), [Norse](/wiki/Saturn%27s_Norse_group_of_satellites "Saturn's Norse group of satellites"), and [Gallic](/wiki/Saturn%27s_Gallic_group_of_satellites "Saturn's Gallic group of satellites") groups, and their names are chosen from the corresponding mythologies the groups are named after. The [rings of Saturn](/wiki/Rings_of_Saturn "Rings of Saturn") are made up of icy objects ranging in size from one centimetre to hundreds of metres, each of which is on its own orbit about the planet. Thus, a precise number of Saturnian moons cannot be given, as there is no objective boundary between the countless small anonymous objects that form Saturn's ring system and the larger objects that have been named as moons. At least 150 "[moonlets](/wiki/Moonlet "Moonlet")" embedded in the rings have been detected by the disturbance they create in the surrounding ring material, though this is thought to be only a small sample of the total population of such objects.

The red grapes in the Bordeaux vineyard are Merlot (62% by area), Cabernet Sauvignon (25%), Cabernet Franc (12%) and a small amount of Petit Verdot, Malbec and Carménère (1% in total). The white grapes are Sémillon (54% by area), Sauvignon blanc (36%), Muscadelle (7%) and a small amount of Ugni blanc, Colombard and Folle blanche (3% in total).[[3]](#cite_note-Bordeaux_Figures-3) Because of the generally humid Bordeaux climate, a variety of pests can cause a problem for the *[vigneron](/wiki/Winemaker "Winemaker")*. The vines are generally [trained](/wiki/Vine_training "Vine training") in either single or double guyot. Mattarella was born in [Palermo](/wiki/Palermo "Palermo") on 23 July 1941 into a prominent [Sicilian](/wiki/Sicilians "Sicilians") family. Bernardo Mattarella has also been accused of being associated with the [Sicilian Mafia](/wiki/Sicilian_Mafia "Sicilian Mafia"); however, accusations were always rejected in court.[[24]](#cite_note-24)[[25]](#cite_note-nyrb041269-25) His mother Maria Buccellato came from an upper-middle-class family of [Trapani](/wiki/Trapani "Trapani").[[26]](#cite_note-26)[[27]](#cite_note-27)

The New York Times :: part 03 :: chunk_0002
The *Times* was founded as the conservative *New-York Daily Times* in 1851, and came to national recognition in the 1870s with its aggressive coverage of corrupt politician [Boss Tweed](/wiki/William_M._Tweed "William M. Tweed"). Following the [Panic of 1893](/wiki/Panic_of_1893 "Panic of 1893"), *[Chattanooga Times](/wiki/Chattanooga_Times "Chattanooga Times")* publisher [Adolph Ochs](/wiki/Adolph_Ochs "Adolph Ochs") gained a controlling interest in the company. In 1935, Ochs was succeeded by his son-in-law, [Arthur Hays Sulzberger](/wiki/Arthur_Hays_Sulzberger "Arthur Hays Sulzberger"), who began a push into European news. Sulzberger's son [Arthur Ochs Sulzberger](/wiki/Arthur_Ochs_Sulzberger "Arthur Ochs Sulzberger") became publisher in 1963, adapting to a changing newspaper industry and introducing radical changes. *The New York Times* was involved in the landmark 1964 [U.S. Supreme Court](/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States") case *[New York Times Co. v. Sullivan](/wiki/New_York_Times_Co._v._Sullivan "New York Times Co. v. Sullivan")*, which restricted the ability of public officials to sue the media for [defamation](/wiki/Defamation "Defamation").

In 1971, *The New York Times* published the *[Pentagon Papers](/wiki/Pentagon_Papers "Pentagon Papers")*, an internal [Department of Defense](/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense "United States Department of Defense") document detailing the [United States's historical involvement](/wiki/United_States_in_the_Vietnam_War "United States in the Vietnam War") in the [Vietnam War](/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War"), despite pushback from then-president [Richard Nixon](/wiki/Richard_Nixon "Richard Nixon"). In the landmark decision *[New York Times Co. v. United States](/wiki/New_York_Times_Co._v._United_States "New York Times Co. v. United States")* (1971), the Supreme Court ruled that the [First Amendment](/wiki/First_Amendment_to_the_United_States_Constitution "First Amendment to the United States Constitution") guaranteed the right to publish the *Pentagon Papers*.
